title: A day accounted for
hook: Seneca gives his day: a cold plunge, a short run, dry bread, a nap (Letters 83)

segments.voice: Yesterday: stage kings and masks. Your line was behind the mask. Whose costume did you look past, and what did you find? Day four hundred seventy-four.
screen: `STAGE KINGS AND MASKS — BEHIND THE MASK.`

segments.voice: Lucilius has asked a simple question: what do you actually do all day? It's the question we ask of anyone whose life we're curious about. What time do you get up? What do you eat? And in the eighty-third letter, Seneca answers it, hour by hour, with surprising honesty, and quite a lot of humor at his own expense. It's the closest thing we have to a day in the life of an aging Roman philosopher, and it's more ordinary than you'd expect. Today: a day accounted for.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU DO ALL DAY?` → `HOUR BY HOUR, HONESTLY.` → `A DAY IN AN OLD PHILOSOPHER'S LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, why tell it. We should live, Seneca says, as if we lived in plain sight, as if God could look into our hearts at any time. So he'll watch himself and review his day, which he calls a most useful practice. Today, he says, is whole: nobody stole any of it. Second, the run. He's taken up a little running, with a young slave named Pharius as his partner. It's a close race, he jokes, since they're both losing teeth now, and he'll soon need a younger runner. Third, the plunge. Seneca was once a great lover of cold water. As a younger man he'd begin the new year with a plunge into the canal. Then he moved to the Tiber. Then to a tub. And now, he confesses, the water has to be warm. That's an old man's honest report. Fourth, the meal and the nap. Lunch is dry bread, with no table needed, and so simple there's no washing of hands afterward. Then a very short nap. Nothing heroic. What's striking is the honesty. He doesn't polish the day. He shows the decline, the jokes, the plain bread. Accounting for a day like that isn't about judging it. It's about seeing where it actually went.
screen: `LIVE AS IF IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · `A RACE WITH PHARIUS.` · `CANAL, RIVER, TUB, WARM WATER.` · `DRY BREAD AND A SHORT NAP.` · then, large: `MY DAY, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Walk back through today so far, the way Seneca does, hour by hour. When did you wake? What came first: the phone, a coffee, a person? What did you eat? Where did the middle of the day go? Don't polish it and don't scold it. Just let the timetable appear, as it really was. Notice one hour that was wholly yours, and one that got stolen. The bell holds the time.
A day accounted for. Seneca's eighty-third letter: a run, a warm-ish plunge, dry bread, a short nap, all reported honestly, to see where the day went. Today's word.
Your line: my day, honestly. Tonight, write today's timetable in a few plain lines, with no polishing. Mark the hour that was wholly yours. Day four hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners write a plain account of their day in the evening, noting where the hours went without praising or scolding themselves.

original.note: Latin: a whole day. Seneca says in Letters 83.3 that today is whole, with nothing stolen from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoics live heroic, ice-cold, iron routines.
what it means: Seneca's day is plain and honestly told; the point is to see where it went.
what a scholar hears: Letters 83.1–6; the daily self-review echoes On Anger 3.36, where Seneca describes examining each day at night, after his teacher Sextius.

notes: Letters 83.1–2: live as if in plain sight, God sees within; 83.2–3 'dies integer est', self-observation and review of the day. 83.4: running with Pharius, both losing teeth. 83.5: from the Euripus (canal) on the Kalends of January, to the Tiber, to a tub, to warm water. 83.6: dry bread, no table, no washing of hands, a very short sleep.
